profile.title: Horace Barlow
profile.extract: Horace Basil Barlow FRS was a British vision scientist.
profile.bio: Horace Basil Barlow FRS (1921–2020) was a British vision scientist and neuroscientist. A great-grandson of Charles Darwin, he read natural sciences at Trinity College, Cambridge and took an M.D. at Harvard (1946). In 1953 he discovered that frog retinal neurons fire selectively to specific visual stimuli, foreshadowing Hubel and Wiesel's work on cortical receptive fields. His 1961 paper on the transformations of sensory messages argued that a central computational aim of the visual system is redundancy reduction — the basis of the efficient coding hypothesis — and he later worked on factorial codes and the statistics of natural scenes. He held posts at Cambridge and UC Berkeley, was elected FRS in 1969, and received the Royal Medal and Australia Prize (both 1993) and the 2009 Swartz Prize for Theoretical and Computational Neuroscience.

profile.extract: Bruno Adolphus Olshausen is an American neuroscientist and professor at the University of California, Berkeley, known for his work on computational neuroscience, vision science, and sparse coding. profile.bio: American neuroscientist, Professor in the Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute and the Herbert Wertheim School of Optometry and Vision Science at UC Berkeley, with an affiliated appointment in EECS, and Director of the Redwood Center for Theoretical Neuroscience. He is best known for showing, with David Field in 1996, that V1 simple-cell receptive fields can emerge from learning a sparse code for natural images. He holds a B.S. and M.S. in Electrical Engineering from Stanford and a Ph.D. in Computation and Neural Systems from Caltech, and held postdocs at Cornell and MIT before joining UC Davis and later UC Berkeley.

profile.extract: Jeffrey Hawkins is an American businessman, computer scientist, neuroscientist and engineer. He co-founded Palm Computing where he co-created the PalmPilot, the Palm Treo and Handspring.

profile.title: Timothy Lillicrap
profile.extract: Timothy P. Lillicrap is a Canadian neuroscientist and artificial intelligence (AI) researcher, adjunct professor at University College London, and staff research scientist at Google DeepMind, where he has been involved in the AlphaGo and AlphaZero projects mastering the games of Go, Chess and Shogi. His research focuses on machine learning and statistics for optimal control and decision making, as well as using these mathematical frameworks to understand how the brain learns. He has developed algorithms and approaches for exploiting deep neural networks in the context of reinforcement learning, and new recurrent memory architectures for one-shot learning.
profile.bio: Canadian neuroscientist and AI researcher, Director of Research at Google DeepMind and adjunct professor at University College London. He works on machine learning and statistics for optimal control and decision-making, and on using those frameworks to understand how the brain learns. He was involved in the AlphaGo and AlphaZero projects, and has developed algorithms for deep reinforcement learning (e.g. DDPG) and recurrent memory architectures for one-shot learning. He holds an Hon. B.Sc. in Cognitive Science & AI from the University of Toronto and a Ph.D. in Systems Neuroscience from Queen's University under Stephen H. Scott; before DeepMind he was a postdoctoral research fellow at Oxford.
